page: Google Cloud Platform n1-highcpu-4 is an x86_64 architecture server belonging to the n1 server family. It is equipped with 4 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 2 physical Intel Xeon cores, utilizing hyperthreading with 2 threads per core. The processor operates at a clock speed of 2.3 GHz and features a 45 MB L3 cache, 0.25 MB L2 cache, and 32 KB L1d cache. System memory totals 4.0 GB, providing a resource density of 0.9 GB of RAM per core. This server does not include bundled local storage or integrated GPUs.

Benchmark evaluations position this instance in the lower performance tiers. The single-core and multi-core CPU performance tests via stress-ng place the server in the bottom 25% of tested hardware. Similarly, Geekbench single-core and multi-core scores fall in the bottom 10% tier. Memory bandwidth tests, including read-only small block cached operations at 162.49 GB/sec and large block uncached write operations at 21.69 GB/sec, consistently rank in the bottom 25%. Cryptography and compression workloads also show limitations, with single-threaded gzip compression registering at 18.99 GB/sec and single-threaded bzip3 decompression at 7.16 GB/sec, both falling into the bottom 10% performance category.

The primary tradeoff of the n1-highcpu-4 is its low memory-to-vCPU ratio, which limits its suitability for memory-intensive applications. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, this instance offers a dedicated compute allocation within an older hardware generation, making it an entry-level option for compute-bound tasks that do not require large memory footprints. It is suited for lightweight web serving, basic software compilation, and minor database operations, as evidenced by its static web serving throughput of 2.92 GB/sec and Redis SET performance of 2.8 million operations per second. It is not suitable for large-scale LLM inference or memory-heavy data processing.

Lacking local storage and GPU accelerators, this instance allocates a low memory-to-core ratio of 0.9 GB per core. Benchmark data indicates entry-level performance, with stress-ng CPU and memory bandwidth results placing the server in the bottom 25% of tested configurations. Similarly, Geekbench and compression tests fall within the bottom 10% to 25% brackets. Given these performance characteristics and the low memory density, this server is best suited for lightweight, compute-bound workloads such as basic software compilation, small-scale database operations, and low-traffic static web serving rather than memory-intensive or modern machine learning tasks.
